The thunder clapped as the light clashed through my billowing curtains. As the wind picked up, the loose papers and dust sprang to life, as if they were animated.

I clung to my loose fitting robe, naked beneath. The chilly air, unusual for summer, swept underneath, tickling my skin in its teasing manner. I was content, in that moment. I tucked the cat away from the storm and approached my open window, the water splaying and coating me in its fingers. Shutting it, I heard a call.

My name.

A friend was outside, sitting beneath the overhang. He just called out, hoping I'd hear. I did. I told him I'd dress and meet him. Lightning cracked again. Throwing on old jeans, a dirty shirt, and my bag, I ran down the flights of steps. I opened the door and embraced him. The thunder grumbled in the midnight air.

He hugged me back. I should have seen then the sadness in his eyes, but I didn't. The only thing I saw was a friend. My friend. But I should have known better. He never calls after midnight unless he was despondent. I would be the only one he would call after those times. Strangely enough, I never called on him.

It'd been about 3 months since I last saw him. We walked into the musty tavern, greeted by the familiar shit music of the degrading culture. We approached the bar. He leaned over, waiting for the bartender to notice him. He asked what I wanted. I looked at him, knowing something was off I felt off too. I would normally have requested a bourbon -- neat-- but tonight was strange. I requested tequila and my trusty Sam Adams.

I watched his face light up. He laughed when I said Sam Adams. I suppose it's not too common. we waited until the beer was poured, the shit music surrounding us. A few familiar faces soared out int he crowd. They knew me as his friend. His friends were all here, so why would he call me?

I knew why, though, while we slammed back out shots, our beers. I was the only one who could see the sadness behind the joking smile. His lady was gone -- they never split. She moved away. And I was the only one who could make him feel normal. So we joked for a bit. We laughed, our ribs hurting from the sudden exposure to rhythm.

But I couldn't be that person for him. He'll not understand, and he likely not remember. I left when he was in the bathroom. The thunder clapped against the dark sky. And I just left. He is my friend. Couldn't let him, or others think we were getting any closer. I don't feel any more than platonic emotions for him, but I know how the devil's water works.

The thunder claps harder, closer while he wonders where I went. It's fine now. No one will remember. But I know I'll always be the one he calls when the storm rolls in. It's no problem. You just have to know when to leave before the lightning hits too close.

A stout slides in front of him, rich with foam.

He looks up to drink, just in time to see the bartender slice an orange. Bartender pinches is it into a shotglass. Bartender picks it up from it's well lit frame on the bar and hands it to the skirt across the way.

Back to his stout. Back to his book.
